overview:
In Jain manuscript culture, "missing folios" refers to the absence, loss, or replacement of individual leaves (pothī‑pages) within a handwritten text. Because most Jain scriptures and scholastic works circulated for centuries in palm‑leaf or paper pothī format, each folio carried a portion of the text, folio numbers, and often marginal notes. When one or more of these leaves are lost, damaged beyond legibility, or substituted at a later date, the integrity of the textual transmission is affected and must be carefully assessed by editors, historians, and religious teachers.

From a material perspective, folios can go missing for many reasons: mechanical wear at the string‑holes, insect damage, water exposure, careless handling during ritual use, or selective removal for art markets when a folio bears an especially attractive miniature. In some cases, as with the Chandonuśāsana manuscript preserved in the Hemacandrācārya Jaina Bhāṇḍāra in Patan, modern photocopies or microfilms themselves omit folios that remain intact in the original, creating a secondary layer of "missing" leaves in the scholarly record even though the physical manuscript is complete. In other cases, such as the Kalpasūtra manuscript MS Add.1765 at Cambridge University Library, individual folios have been replaced—folio 84 is a modern insertion, and the final folio (with the colophon) is an older replacement—indicating that earlier leaves were lost and later scribes or owners supplied new ones.

Textually, missing folios can interrupt narrative sequences, doctrinal expositions, or lists of rules. For canonical texts like the Kalpasūtra, which combine biography, doctrinal summaries, and monastic regulations, the loss of a folio may remove part of a Jina’s life story or a segment of the Sāmācārī (rules for the rainy‑season retreat). Critical editors reconstruct such gaps by collating multiple manuscripts, comparing parallel recensions, and marking lacunae explicitly in printed editions. When a folio is replaced, its script, paper, ink, and orthography often differ from the surrounding leaves, and careful palaeographic analysis is needed to determine whether the replacement faithfully transmits the original text or introduces variant readings.

Within Jain traditions, missing folios are not merely a technical issue but also a devotional and ritual concern. Illuminated Kalpasūtra manuscripts and narrative addenda like the Kalakācārya‑kathā have long been objects of worship, public recitation, and display during festivals such as Paryuṣaṇa. When a manuscript used in ritual is incomplete, communities may commission new copies or rely on other complete exemplars for liturgical reading, while preserving the older, damaged manuscript as a revered artifact. Scholars of Jain history and art must therefore distinguish between ritual completeness (having enough text for liturgical use) and philological completeness (preserving every original folio).

From the standpoint of modern textual criticism, missing folios highlight the layered nature of Jain scriptural transmission. They remind us that no single manuscript can be treated as an infallible witness; instead, editors must work with families of manuscripts, noting where folios are absent, replaced, or mis‑ordered. They also expose the limits of our knowledge: when all surviving witnesses lack a particular passage because the relevant folios were lost early in the tradition, reconstruction becomes speculative and must be clearly labeled as such. For students of Jainism, understanding missing folios encourages a humble approach to claims about "original" wording and invites consultation with qualified scholars and lineage‑holders when doctrinal or ritual decisions depend on contested textual segments.

Finally, the phenomenon of missing folios intersects with broader questions of preservation ethics. Decisions about conservation, digitization, and display can either mitigate or exacerbate the risk of further loss. Responsible custodianship involves documenting the current state of each manuscript, including any missing or replacement folios, and making this information available in catalogues and digital libraries. In this way, both Jain communities and academic researchers can navigate the tension between honoring manuscripts as sacred objects and treating them as historical sources whose gaps, silences, and repairs must be critically interpreted.

primary_sources.title: Kalpasūtra (MS Add.1765, Cambridge University Library)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu
primary_sources.translation: ... folio 84 is a new leaf, written in place of the earlier leaf ...
primary_sources.notes: This line represents the kind of descriptive note found in modern catalogues and scholarly discussions of the Kalpasūtra manuscript MS Add.1765, where folio 84 is identified as a recent replacement and the final folio as an older substitution. The primary Prakrit text of the Kalpasūtra itself does not comment on missing folios; instead, material evidence—differences in paper, ink, and script—reveals that certain leaves were lost and later replaced. Cataloguers and editors then paraphrase this situation in Sanskrit or English to document the manuscript’s condition. In this example, the wording is a synthetic, illustrative paraphrase rather than a verbatim quotation from a colophon, and it should be read as an interpretive summary of the manuscript description rather than as canonical scripture.

primary_sources.title: Chandonuśāsana manuscript A (Hemacandrācārya Jaina Bhāṇḍāra, Patan, Cat. No. 110-2)
primary_sources.author: Vāgbhaṭa (with self‑commentary Vivaraṇa)
primary_sources.original_text: … kecid granthapattrāṇi lipikāra‑dṛṣṭyā na pratilikhitāni, tasmāt pratilipau pattrāntara‑bhāvaḥ dṛśyate …
primary_sources.transliteration: ... kecid grantha-pattrāṇi lipikāra-dṛṣṭyā na pratilikhitāni, tasmāt pratilipau pattrāntara-bhāvaḥ dṛśyate ...
primary_sources.translation: ... certain manuscript leaves were not copied by the scribe, therefore in the photocopy an absence of leaves is seen ...
primary_sources.notes: The International Journal of Jaina Studies article on Vāgbhaṭa’s Chandonuśāsana describes how the modern photocopy of manuscript A is missing some folios, even though those folios remain intact in the original palm‑leaf manuscript. The sentence above is an interpretive Sanskrit paraphrase of that modern scholarly observation, not a direct quotation from the manuscript itself. It illustrates the distinction between the physical completeness of the original Jain manuscript and the secondary incompleteness of its reproduction, a key example of how "missing folios" can arise at different stages of transmission. Editors preparing a critical edition must therefore consult the original, not only the photocopy, to avoid mistaking reproduction gaps for ancient textual lacunae.

misconceptions.myth: Missing folios always indicate deliberate censorship or doctrinal suppression in Jain scripture.
misconceptions.reality: In most documented cases, missing folios result from physical damage, routine wear, or accidental omission during copying or reproduction, rather than intentional removal of doctrinally sensitive material. While it is theoretically possible that a leaf could be removed for ideological reasons, responsible scholarship requires concrete evidence—such as explicit notes, parallel manuscripts preserving the omitted passage, or historical records—before making such claims. The default explanation in Jain manuscript studies is material loss, not purposeful censorship.

misconceptions.myth: If a single revered manuscript of a Jain text has missing folios, the lost content can be confidently reconstructed from memory or oral tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Reconstruction of missing folio content is a careful, probabilistic process based on collating multiple manuscripts, comparing parallel recensions, and analyzing internal structure. Even when oral recitation traditions exist, they themselves may have been shaped by written exemplars that already contained gaps. As a result, any attempt to fill a lacuna must be clearly marked as conjectural and cannot be treated as binding or universally authoritative. For doctrinal or ritual decisions that hinge on such reconstructed passages, consultation with qualified ācāryas and scholars from the relevant Jain lineage is essential.

misconceptions.myth: A manuscript with missing or replacement folios is spiritually invalid and should not be used in Jain ritual or study.
misconceptions.reality: Jain communities often continue to honor and use manuscripts that have suffered damage or undergone repair, especially when they are historically important or artistically significant. Ritual practice may rely on other complete copies for recitation while still venerating incomplete manuscripts as sacred objects. From a scholarly perspective, even damaged or partially preserved manuscripts can provide valuable evidence about textual history, art, and devotional life. Spiritual validity in Jainism is not mechanically tied to the physical perfection of a single manuscript folio.

misconceptions.myth: Modern printed editions automatically eliminate all problems caused by missing folios in older Jain manuscripts.
misconceptions.reality: Critical editions can mitigate the impact of missing folios by drawing on multiple witnesses and marking lacunae, but they cannot restore text that has disappeared from all surviving manuscript traditions. If every known manuscript family lacks a particular segment because the relevant folios were lost early, editors must acknowledge that the original wording is irretrievable. Printed books may therefore contain silent gaps or editorial conjectures, and readers should pay attention to prefaces, apparatus, and scholarly notes that explain where missing folios have shaped the transmitted text.
